common_name: Hong Kong Kumquat (Hong Kong Wild Kumquat)

planting.note: Plant grafted or rooted-cutting stock in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, or grow in a container to shelter indoors in winter; Hong Kong kumquat tolerates light frost once established but is best treated as tender outside zones 9-11.

directions: Plant grafted or rooted-cutting stock in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, or grow in a container to shelter indoors in winter; Hong Kong kumquat tolerates light frost once established but is best treated as tender outside zones 9-11. This dense, twiggy, thorny shrub from the rocky hillsides of southern China and Hong Kong bears masses of tiny, pea- to marble-sized round fruit with thin, sweet, edible rind wrapped around intensely tart, seedy pulp, best nibbled whole rather than juiced. It flowers and fruits abundantly even as a small potted specimen, making it a popular choice for bonsai and container citrus collections as much as for the fruit itself, and its fine, small-leaved habit distinguishes it from the larger-leaved kumquats grown for eating fresh. Feed with a citrus fertilizer through the growing season, water deeply but infrequently, and prune lightly after fruiting to maintain shape.
sources: University of California Riverside Citrus Variety Collection
Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, raised or mounded soil in full sun with cold-air drainage; Armstrong satsuma is among the more cold-hardy satsuma selections and is a Gulf South dooryard favorite from Louisiana to coastal Texas.

directions: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, raised or mounded soil in full sun with cold-air drainage; Armstrong satsuma is among the more cold-hardy satsuma selections and is a Gulf South dooryard favorite from Louisiana to coastal Texas. A bud-sport selection of Owari satsuma found in the Gulf South, it produces the same sweet, easy-peeling, nearly seedless fruit but ripens two to three weeks earlier, letting growers harvest ahead of the season's first hard freeze in marginal citrus climates. The compact, glossy-leaved, thornless tree is heavily productive and, like other satsumas, hardier to cold than most other mandarins, tolerating brief dips into the low 20s Fahrenheit once mature. Mulch the root zone and wrap or cover young trees during hard freezes, and pick fruit as soon as it colors since satsumas hold poorly on the tree once ripe.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in dry to average, humus-rich, acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; white-tinged sedge is more drought-tolerant in dry shade than most native sedges and establishes readily from divisions.

directions: Plant divisions in spring or fall in dry to average, humus-rich, acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; white-tinged sedge is more drought-tolerant in dry shade than most native sedges and establishes readily from divisions. Fine, wiry, arching blue-green leaves form small, tidy tufts that spread gradually into a loose, informal groundcover under oaks and pines, with inconspicuous flower spikes in spring that give way to small, pale, silvery-tinged seed heads. It is among the more drought-tough native sedges once established, tolerating the dry, root-filled soil of established woodland far better than moisture-loving sedge species, and needs no mowing, fertilizing, or irrigation in a naturalized planting. Use it as a fine-textured lawn substitute or filler between larger shade perennials in dry woodland gardens.

planting.note: Plant divisions or plugs in spring in average to dry, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Bicknell's sedge is a prairie and savanna native that adapts to average garden soil once established.

directions: Plant divisions or plugs in spring in average to dry, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Bicknell's sedge is a prairie and savanna native that adapts to average garden soil once established. Clumps of narrow, medium-green foliage send up wiry stems in late spring topped with plump, oval, straw-colored seed heads tinged coppery-brown at maturity, giving the plant strong textural interest well beyond its bloom period. Native to tallgrass prairies, savannas, and open woodland edges across the central and eastern United States, it combines well with prairie wildflowers and grasses in a naturalistic planting or rain garden and provides seed for songbirds through fall and winter. It tolerates both the dry conditions of prairie plantings and the light shade of savanna edges, needing no supplemental water once its root system is established.

planting.note: Plant divisions or potted plugs in spring in wet to consistently moist, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun at pond edges, rain gardens, or bog gardens; bearded sedge tolerates several inches of standing water as well as ordinary moist garden soil.

directions: Plant divisions or potted plugs in spring in wet to consistently moist, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun at pond edges, rain gardens, or bog gardens; bearded sedge tolerates several inches of standing water as well as ordinary moist garden soil. Broad, arching, bright green leaves form a bold clump from which tall stems rise in early summer bearing distinctive, spiky, drooping seed heads with long bristled scales that give the plant its shaggy, bottlebrush-like common name. Native to marshes, wet meadows, and pond and stream margins across much of North America, it is an excellent structural accent for the wet edge of a water garden or bioswale, offering strong textural contrast to broad-leaved emergent plants like pickerelweed and arrowhead. It spreads slowly by short rhizomes and self-sows in consistently wet ground, forming loose colonies over time without becoming aggressive.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Chinese box orange tolerates poor, sandy, and salt-affected soils and is commonly grown as a dense, thorny hedge in coastal and southern landscapes.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Chinese box orange tolerates poor, sandy, and salt-affected soils and is commonly grown as a dense, thorny hedge in coastal and southern landscapes. This slow-growing, densely branched citrus relative carries small, glossy, boxwood-like leaves on stiff, thorny stems, with tiny, fragrant white flowers followed by small, dark, olive-black berries that are not palatable but are eaten by birds. Its dense, twiggy, thorn-armed growth makes it an outstanding impenetrable barrier hedge or foundation screen, and it shears well to a formal shape, tolerating heat, drought, and salt spray once established far better than most true citrus. Prune after the main spring flush to maintain a tight hedge form and remove any wayward growth.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; limeberry is frost-tender and best suited to sheltered dooryard plantings in zones 9b-11 or large containers moved indoors for winter further north.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; limeberry is frost-tender and best suited to sheltered dooryard plantings in zones 9b-11 or large containers moved indoors for winter further north. This small, thorny, trifoliate-leaved citrus relative bears intensely fragrant, orange-blossom-scented white flowers nearly year-round in frost-free climates, followed by small, oval, deep-red fruit with a sweet, thin skin over lime-tart, mucilaginous pulp traditionally used in preserves and candies rather than eaten fresh. Long grown as a dooryard and hedge plant across the tropics and subtropics, it tolerates shearing well and makes a fragrant, fine-textured, thorny barrier planting or specimen shrub near a patio where its flower scent can be enjoyed. Protect from frost, water regularly during dry spells, and prune lightly after flushes of bloom to maintain shape.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products
